analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue manufacturers that cut off stores for selling at a discount.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote in October 1991 with 89 cosponsors from both parties, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Some manufacturers pressure stores to charge a minimum price by cutting off discounters who sell too cheap. A Supreme Court ruling had made these cases hard to win because it was difficult to prove the manufacturer and a competitor secretly coordinated. This bill would let a jury infer an illegal price agreement when a supplier, after hearing from a competitor, drops a store for its low prices — and would make even an unwritten price agreement between a supplier and a dealer a violation of antitrust law.
analysis.who_benefits: Price-cutting retailers — especially small and independent stores and discounters — who could sue when they are dropped by suppliers for undercutting the approved price. Shoppers benefit too, because the bill is aimed at keeping discount pricing alive rather than letting manufacturers prop up uniform retail prices.

how_it_helps.text: If a supplier gets a communication from a competitor about a store's price competition and then terminates or refuses to supply that store, a jury may infer the supplier and competitor acted together to fix resale prices [S3] [S4].

A supplier-purchaser agreement to set resale prices would itself be a violation, and an agreement to cut off a dealer over its pricing would be a violation even if no specific price was agreed to [S3] [S4].
These rules would apply to civil cases already filed when the bill became law [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and brand-name suppliers, including pharmaceutical and other consumer-goods makers, would lose the ability to enforce minimum resale prices and would face more lawsuits. Their authorized dealer networks would lose the price-floor protection that keeps their margins up.
analysis.who_pays_short: Manufacturers and their authorized dealer networks

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to lawsuits filed before its enactment [S3] [S4], changing the rules for cases already in court — a fairness objection any honest supporter would have to answer.

Manufacturers argued in good faith that minimum-price policies protect small full-service dealers who provide demonstrations and service, and that making evidence easier to use could chill legitimate decisions to drop a dealer — the House added a defense for defendants too small to have market power to address this [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core purpose — letting juries connect a supplier's punishing of a price-cutter with a competitor's complaint — addresses a real enforcement gap for discounters and their customers. The retroactive application to pending cases was its weakest design feature, and the small-market-power defense partially answered concerns about sweeping in minor players. On balance it favored price competition over margin protection.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House by voice vote on October 10, 1991, but was set aside pending a companion Senate bill that the Senate never voted on, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced March 19, 1991, by Rep. Jack Brooks and referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S6].
It cleared subcommittee and full committee markups and was reported out on October 3, 1991 [S6].
The House passed it by voice vote on October 10, 1991, after which it was laid on the table with further action tied to the companion Senate bill S. 429 [S6].
The Senate never acted, and the bill died at the end of the 102nd Congress in January 1993 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and brand-name suppliers who enforce minimum retail prices came out ahead: the House-passed crackdown died without the Senate ever taking a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Manufacturers that enforce minimum retail prices

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 75 Democrats, 13 Republicans, and 1 Independent among 89 cosponsors — and the House passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded party roll call [S5] [S6].

industries.industry: Manufacturers and brand-name suppliers (including pharmaceutical and consumer-goods makers)
industries.note: They would lose the ability to enforce minimum resale prices and would face easier lawsuits for cutting off discounters. Their gain from the bill's death was the public's loss, since uniform price floors keep discount pricing down.

industries.industry: Discount retailers and small independent dealers
industries.note: They could sue suppliers who cut them off for undercutting the approved price, which lets them keep selling cheap and keeps discount options open for shoppers.
Networks built on price-floor protection would face more lawsuits, though the bill left territorial and location restraints under the looser rule-of-reason standard [S4].
